did_you_know.text: Did you know? Tamar was Absalom’s sister and David’s daughter, while Amnon was David’s son. Thus, the story is portrayed as a tragedy within the royal family itself.
Did you know? Jonadab, Amnon’s adviser, was the son of Shimeah, David’s brother, and the text calls him “a very shrewd man.”
Did you know? David himself sent Tamar to Amnon’s house to prepare food for him after Amnon pretended to be sick.
Did you know? Tamar tried to prevent the assault by arguing that such an act was “a disgrace in Israel,” and she even suggested that Amnon ask the king for her.
Did you know? After assaulting Tamar, Amnon began to hate her intensely—even more intensely than the love he had supposedly felt for her. The text emphasizes the perversion of his “love.”
Did you know? Tamar expressed her grief publicly: she put ashes on her head, tore her richly ornamented robe, placed her hand on her head, and walked away crying out.
Did you know? David heard about what had happened and was furious, but these verses do not describe him taking action. Absalom, however, kept his hatred for Amnon to himself.
Did you know? Absalom waited two full years before acting against Amnon. The opportunity arose at the sheep-shearing festival at Baal Hazor, to which he invited the king’s sons.
Did you know? After Amnon’s death, David received the false report that all the king’s sons had been killed. Jonadab corrected the report, explaining that only Amnon had died.
Did you know? Absalom fled to Geshur and remained there for three years. Geshur was the kingdom of Talmai son of Ammihud, Maakah’s father and Absalom’s maternal grandfather.
